topic: Degraded Performance for Multiple Models: An Outage Postmortem

key_points: Official Anthropic postmortem (2025-09-17): three separate infrastructure bugs silently degraded Claude response quality between August and early September 2025 — no server-side error fired for any of them.

Bug 1, context-window routing error: introduced Aug 5, ~0.8% of Sonnet 4 requests; at the worst hour on Aug 31, 16% of Sonnet 4 requests were affected and ~30% of Claude Code users during that window had at least one message routed to the wrong server type. Sticky routing made follow-ups likely to hit the same bad server. Bedrock peaked at 0.18%; Vertex AI under 0.0004% (Aug 27–Sep 16). Fix: routing logic corrected Sep 4; rolled out to first-party and Vertex by Sep 16, Bedrock by Sep 18.

Bug 2, output corruption: misconfiguration deployed to Claude API TPU servers on Aug 25 caused wrong tokens (Thai/Chinese characters inside English answers, obvious syntax errors). Affected Opus 4.1/4 on Aug 25–28 and Sonnet 4 on Aug 25–Sep 2. Third-party platforms unaffected.

Bug 3, approximate top-k XLA:TPU miscompilation: an Aug 25 code change to token selection triggered a latent XLA:TPU compiler bug, confirmed affecting Haiku 3.5 and believed to touch a subset of Sonnet 4 and Opus 3.

Diagnosis was slow because the bugs overlapped and because a load-balancing change on Aug 29 (after the bugs landed) increased affected traffic, so some users saw failures while others saw normal performance — contradictory reports that looked like normal feedback variation.
Explicit vendor denial worth quoting: 'We never reduce model quality due to demand, time of day, or server load. The problems our users reported were due to infrastructure bugs alone.'

FailureAtlas (arXiv 2607.17525, 2026-07-20): a two-axis taxonomy of failures in multi-provider LLM gateway/serving infrastructure — origin layer (Network/Transport, Streaming/Protocol, State/Session, Model Behavior, Governance/Cost) x detectability (Loud vs Silent).

Principal finding: the most operationally severe failures are silent — they return HTTP 200, pass every standard health check, and corrupt application state; detecting them requires semantic-level observability, not latency/error-rate/uptime monitoring.

First-hand silent failure #1: a concurrency race in conversation-state management — two coroutines read history, append a turn, and write back; the second write silently overwrites the first. Turns vanish from the context window, generation quality degrades, every request still returns HTTP 200, and no latency/error/pod-health metric registers an anomaly. Found only because a semantic continuity benchmark showed persona-adherence drops under high concurrency.

First-hand silent failure #2: a streaming index collision that corrupts tool-call payloads. Also documented: a retry storm where 100 parallel agents retried on a fixed interval, synchronised into a thundering herd that saturated the provider's rate limit on every retry window — 25% of requests failed permanently from a momentary 502.

Reported negative finding: the authors could not find a single evidence-grade, reproducible bug report of an infrastructure-level failure in model behaviour — 'a legitimate finding, not a gap in our survey' — meaning most 'the model got dumber' claims are unproven.
Governance/control-plane mechanisms are designed and tested against the happy path, so they are most likely to malfunction exactly when the upstream provider is degraded worst.

Tail latency (p90/p95/p99) is what users actually experience; average latency can look healthy while p99 sits at 12 seconds. 'If you are only watching mean response time, you are watching the wrong number.'
Time to First Token (TTFT) needs its own dashboard — a model that streams fast but takes 3s to start feels broken even with excellent throughput.
Queue depth is a leading indicator of tail-latency degradation: by the time utilisation crosses a threshold the queue has already grown and p99 has already spiked.
Cold-start latency decomposes into model-weight loading, LoRA adapter initialisation, KV-cache allocation, and container startup — each needs separate instrumentation.
The model is rarely the bottleneck: teams optimise inference time and then find CPU preprocessing and tokenisation add more latency than the GPU step they just optimised.
Tracing practice: tail-based sampling — capture 100% of requests above p99 and 100% of errors, but sample routine fast requests at 1–5%.

OpenAI's own troubleshooting guidance: filter before investigating — always to a single model (issues on low-traffic models are hidden by high-volume traffic; high-volume models make localised issues look global), to one service tier, and to the affected project. Selecting multiple models aggregates, it does not switch between them.

Use the HTTP Requests view, not the Uptime tab, and interpret error rates rather than raw error counts. If client-side errors appear with no corresponding Service Health data, the requests likely never reached OpenAI — the fault is upstream (timeouts, proxies, networking).

Use percentiles, not averages, for latency analysis; latency analysis is most meaningful on priority and scale tiers that have defined SLAs (standard tier has no guaranteed latency). Key metrics: Token Velocity (tokens/sec, independent of prompt size) and Request Time.
Service Health Dashboard is currently available only to Enterprise API customers — a monitoring-capability gap for everyone else.
OpenAI's own status history aggregated (source status.openai.com): 112 OpenAI outages since January 27, 2026 — the dominant incident type is not total outage but degraded performance.

May 15–16, 2026 'GPT5.5 Performance Degradation': investigating posted May 15 16:11 UTC, mitigation May 16 00:35 UTC, resolved May 17 00:15 UTC — a multi-day degraded window on a single flagship model.

May 19–20, 2026: elevated errors for GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.5 with Chat Completions and Responses both marked 'Degraded performance'; detected and mitigated within roughly an hour, resolved to Operational by 00:37 UTC.
April 23, 2026 Codex gpt-5.5: intermittent 'not found' errors across VS Code extension, Codex API, Codex Web, CLI and App — all five components marked 'Degraded performance'.

Provider-degradation alert thresholds that practitioners actually use: P95 TTFT above 3s → warning (degraded performance); error rate above 5% → warning; error rate above 20% → critical page; 503/504 on 3+ consecutive checks → switch to backup provider; rate-limit utilisation above 70% → warning.
Sudden spikes in p95 TTFT are often the first signal of upstream provider degradation, arriving before it escalates to a full outage.
Monitoring is proactive, failover is reactive — you want to know about an OpenAI p95 TTFT move from 600ms to 4s before users notice, even while every request technically succeeds.

stats.fact: Anthropic's three-bug cascade: at its worst hour on Aug 31, 2025, 16% of Sonnet 4 requests were affected, and about 30% of Claude Code users in that period had at least one message routed to the wrong server type — while the API still returned successful responses.
stats.source: Anthropic Engineering, 'A postmortem of three recent issues', 2025-09-17

stats.fact: The first Anthropic bug was introduced on Aug 5, 2025 and affected roughly 0.8% of Sonnet 4 requests; a load-balancing change on Aug 29 then increased affected traffic, turning a narrow bug into visible, contradictory user reports.
OpenAI's status page recorded 112 outages since January 27, 2026, overwhelmingly 'degraded performance' incidents rather than full outages.

The May 15–17, 2026 GPT-5.5 performance degradation ran about 32 hours — the longest single OpenAI event that month — while the API layer still advertised 99.98% uptime over the 90 days ending May 2026 (broader system 99.84%).

On July 25, 2026 OpenAI's API, ChatGPT and Codex failed simultaneously across 31 service components and took 1h51m to fully restore; third-party monitoring showed OpenAI had no fully normal day for 17 consecutive days (two major outages plus a run of degraded-performance and partial-outage days).

Anthropic's April 23, 2026 postmortem admitted three product-layer changes degraded Opus 4.7 coding quality: reasoning effort silently lowered high→medium on March 4 (reverted April 7), and a March 26 prompt-caching optimisation that wiped prior thinking on every turn after idle sessions instead of once (fixed April 10).

OpenAI Codex lead Thibault Sottiaux acknowledged on May 15, 2026 that two bugs had degraded GPT-5.5 capability in Codex over the previous ~48 hours, then confirmed the fix and 'stable and recovered' the next day — acknowledgement to closure inside 24 hours.
An InsightFinder analysis found 91% of production LLMs experience silent behavioural drift within 90 days of deployment.

A documented May 2026 production case: a support agent returned wrong answers on roughly 1 in 14 requests for nine days while every infrastructure dashboard stayed green; cost was about $97/day in token burn plus downstream cost of incorrect actions. Root cause: health checks, not behavioural drift detectors.
stats.source: Prefactor, 'Canary evaluation for production AI agents'

stats.fact: Canary-eval alert tiers in production use: a 2–3% score drop below the rolling seven-day baseline triggers investigation, 5% or more triggers a priority alert, and 10% across two consecutive canary runs triggers a circuit breaker / rollback. Lloyds Banking Group is cited as the source of the 2%/5% thresholds.
stats.source: Prefactor via Lloyds Banking Group practice, 2025–2026

stats.fact: A 2025 structured-prompt-drift study measured 23% variance in response length for GPT-4 across rolling 2,250-response samples, with 31% instruction-following inconsistency for Mixtral over the same window.

In a longitudinal study of a production LLM agent runtime (8 LLM providers, ~40 scheduled jobs, 4,286 unit tests, 827 governance checks), 22 incidents over eight weeks all had a silent phase; a single meta-pattern — an error signal that never reaches a human in actionable form — manifested at least 28 times.

A canary that tracks a model against itself screened 2,336 GPQA Diamond / MMLU-Pro / competition-math / AIME questions (4 samples each); ~93% were answered correctly first try and 97% of questions turned out to be always-right or always-wrong, leaving only 78 'sometimes right' questions with the statistical power to detect a real regression.

Azure AI Foundry customers reported gpt-5-mini tokens/second degrading until the same job took 90–120s versus 60s worst-case before, while a newer model completed it in under 20s; Microsoft attributed this to shared-capacity queueing, regional demand and concurrency — not intentional throttling.

A May 18, 2026 Azure Q&A thread documented sudden latency increases with no customer-side change and consistent token volume, which the analysis attributed to a silent backend change — model version update, infrastructure rebalancing, or increased shared-tenant load — with no official incident on the health dashboard.

angles: The postmortem-genre angle: the best model-degradation postmortems now come from the vendors themselves (Anthropic's three-bug cascade, the April 2026 Opus 4.7 admission, OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Codex bugs). Teach readers to mine vendor postmortems as a free reliability syllabus — and to notice what they leave out.

Degradation is not outage: the status page's green dot measures a different thing than your users feel. 'Far more yellow than red' — 99.9% raw uptime can coexist with a terrible latency week, and 'useful uptime' (a completed response under your latency bar) diverges hard at peak.

The silent-failure class: HTTP 200 with broken output. FailureAtlas's central finding plus the 91%-drift-in-90-days stat make the case that latency/error/uptime monitoring is structurally blind to the failures that matter most.

A postmortem taxonomy you can reuse: classify any degradation incident on two axes — origin layer (network/transport, streaming/protocol, state/session, model behaviour, governance/cost) and detectability (loud vs silent) — and pick the detection instrument that matches the cell.

Timeline reconstruction is the hard part, and it fails when the harness drifts: pin the CLI/tool version, system-prompt hash, sampling params and model id, or a changed harness looks exactly like a changed model and you spend the postmortem arguing instead of fixing.

Separate real regression from sampling noise: aggregate averages and a handful of bad prompts prove nothing. Use a frozen 'sometimes-right' question panel, paired per-item statistics, a control arm, and pre-registered decision rules.

Self-inflicted amplification: during multi-model degradation, naive retries and eager failover become the incident — the FailureAtlas retry storm turned a momentary 502 into 25% permanent failures across 100 agents.

Detection latency is the metric that actually matters: OpenAI closed GPT-5.5-in-Codex degradation in ~24 hours while Anthropic's overlapping bugs took weeks to even diagnose, because contradictory reports looked like normal feedback variation.

The compliance/contract angle: your provider's status-page definition of 'degraded performance' is the definition that decides whether you get SLA credit — build your own useful-uptime SLI before the incident, not after.
